newsitem.title: FRANCE: Paris fashion designers in, out of revolving doors.
newsitem.headline: Paris fashion designers in, out of revolving doors.

text.p: Leading French fashion houses are engaged in a high-stakes game of designer-swapping, setting in motion a new round of musical chairs as the Paris Spring-Summer ready-to-wear shows prepare to open on Monday.

All eyes will be on the distinguished fashion empire of luxury goods giant LVMH, where Christian Dior and Givenchy are changing creative directors, and a question mark hangs over the fate of the flamboyant Christian Lacroix.

British and French media say John Galliano, the mischievious Briton appointed at Givenchy last year, is set to be transferred to Christian Dior to replace Italian Gianfranco Ferre, who stages his last show there on Tuesday.
His Givenchy job, they believe, will go to another iconoclastic Briton, Alexander McQueen.
Dior and Givenchy refused comment.
"The announcement will be made in the week of October 14. No official confirmation will be made before then," Dior spokesman Bernard Danillon said.
"LVMH is interested in new creative forces," he said, adding that important changes were also expected in LVMH's other fashion firms such as Celine, Kenzo and Louis Vuitton.
LVMH chief Bernard Arnault gave the strongest hint that Galliano will go to Dior by buying his fashion house and putting in Dior president Francois Baufume to run it.
In just three catwalk collections, Galliano had turned Givenchy's prim and proper classics into some of the sexiest, most dramatic clothes to be found.
It is a hard act to follow and the fashion press is betting that McQueen, Britain's nasty boy, will get the challenge of sustaining Givenchy's exciting but precarious new image.
But, in an interview with the U.S.-based trade newspaper Women's Wear Daily, he didn't sound too thrilled.

"I think it's ridiculous the way it's being handled. They're telling all the designers not to talk, but you can't keep a secret in the fashion world. It's putting alot of pressure on me that I don't need right now," McQueen, 27, said.

He seemed worried that working for Givenchy would take too much of his attention away from his own label. "My first concern has to be McQueen. Givenchy would be a lot of money but I'm not into that. Plus, Paris does nothing for me."
Indicating that he had been talking to Givenchy, McQueen said: "They haven't made up their minds and neither have I."

Lacroix, a member of the LVMH pack since 1987, has reason to hope he may finally placate Arnault by making a profit after years of losses. Lacroix's two new lines -- Bazaar and Jeans -- boosted sales by 50 percent in 1995.
Guy Laroche fashion house, owned by Groupe Bic, is also in a state of flux. American designer Alber Elbaz has just been named to replace Michel Klein, whose contract expired in March.
Elbaz, 35, has been Geoffrey Beene's right-hand man in New York for the past seven years. His first luxury ready-to-wear line for Guy Laroche will be shown in March 1997.

One of the season's key events is that Yves Saint Laurent is abandoning the catwalk after more than thirty years. He will present his fashions by appointment only in small private showings at his headquarters.

"The increasing number of shows, their geographic dispersal, intolerable delays, coordination and organisation difficulties do not allow us to present our collections to the press and professional buyers in a fitting manner," Yves Saint Laurent Couture president Pierre Berge said in a statement.
Collections by 87 designers are on the official 10-day schedule with another 41 showing by appointment.
